fact: The A80 Supra's 2JZ-GTE engine became legendary for its ability to handle over 1,000hp with minimal modifications — making it one of the most tuned engines in history.
The 993 was the last air-cooled 911 Porsche ever made — widely considered by enthusiasts to be the purest and most beautiful 911 of all time.
The FD RX-7 is one of the lightest sports cars of its era, and the only mass-production car of the 1990s powered by a twin-turbocharged rotary engine.
The Testarossa's iconic side strakes weren't just styling — they channelled air to the massive side-mounted radiators needed to cool its wide flat-12 engine.
The original Mustang sold over 1 million units in its first 18 months — a record that had never been seen in the automotive industry before.
The Countach's scissor doors and wedge shape were so radical that the word 'countach' — a Piedmontese exclamation of astonishment — became its name after designer Gandini first sketched it.
The R34 GT-R was officially rated at 280hp due to a gentlemen's agreement between Japanese manufacturers — but independent tests consistently showed it producing closer to 330hp.
The E30 M3 was built primarily to go racing — BMW needed to homologate it for touring car competitions, which is why it has a completely different engine from the standard 3 Series.
At just 725kg, the Lotus Elise weighs less than half of most modern SUVs — and its revolutionary bonded aluminium chassis was so innovative it influenced how sports cars are built to this day.
The original Viper had no roof, no side windows, no ABS, no traction control, and no airbags — Dodge intentionally built it as a raw, dangerous driving experience.
Ayrton Senna personally helped develop the NSX's chassis, pushing Honda engineers to make it stiffer — his input directly shaped one of the greatest driver's cars ever built.
The AE86 became a legend through drifting culture and the manga Initial D — despite being an economy car with modest power, its light weight and perfect balance made it a grassroots motorsport icon.
The Z32 300ZX was so technologically advanced that it won Motor Trend's Import Car of the Year in 1990 — and its twin-turbo VG30DETT engine became a tuner favorite.
Colin McRae's legendary WRC wins in the Impreza turned the humble Subaru brand into a rally icon overnight — the road car's boxer rumble became the soundtrack of 1990s motorsport.
Tommi Mäkinen drove the Evo VI to win the 1999 WRC Drivers' Championship — making it four consecutive titles and cementing the Evo as the ultimate rally weapon of its era.
The S2000's F20C engine revved to 9,000 RPM and produced 120hp per litre — the highest specific output of any naturally aspirated production engine at the time of its release.
The S13 Silvia became the definitive drift car in Japan — its perfect weight balance and responsive SR20DET engine made it the weapon of choice for an entire generation of drift drivers.
The NA MX-5 single-handedly revived the affordable roadster segment — its design was inspired by the Lotus Elan, and it went on to become the best-selling two-seat sports car in history.

The S30 Fairlady Z (sold as the Datsun 240Z in the West) proved that Japan could build a world-class sports car — it outsold every European rival and changed perceptions of Japanese engineering forever.
The EK9 Civic Type R's B16B engine produced 185hp from just 1.6 litres naturally aspirated — a feat of engineering that required hand-ported intake ports and a screaming 8,200 RPM redline.
The SW20 MR2 Turbo was nicknamed the 'poor man's Ferrari' — its mid-engine layout and snap-oversteer character earned it both respect and fear in equal measure.
The LFA's 4.8L V10 was co-developed with Yamaha and revs to 9,000 RPM so fast that a conventional tachometer couldn't keep up — Lexus had to use a digital one instead.
When the R35 GT-R launched, it demolished the Nürburgring lap record for production cars — embarrassing supercars costing three times its price and earning the nickname 'Godzilla'.
The 2000GT was Japan's first supercar and starred in the 1967 James Bond film 'You Only Live Twice' — Toyota built a special open-top version because Sean Connery was too tall for the coupe.
The E46 M3's S54 inline-six is widely regarded as one of the greatest engines BMW ever built — its 8,000 RPM redline and linear power delivery made it the benchmark sports sedan of its era.

The 300SL was the first production car with fuel injection and its iconic gullwing doors weren't a styling choice — the tubular spaceframe chassis was so high-sided that conventional doors were impossible.
The original Quattro revolutionised rallying — when it debuted in the WRC, rivals were so outclassed that every serious team was forced to develop their own four-wheel-drive systems to compete.
The 944 Turbo achieved near-perfect 50:50 weight distribution by mounting its engine at the front and its transaxle at the rear — making it one of the best-handling Porsches ever built.
The original Golf GTI invented the hot hatchback segment — Volkswagen initially planned to build just 5,000 units, but demand was so overwhelming they couldn't build them fast enough.
The 2002 Turbo was Europe's first turbocharged production car — and its reversed 'Turbo' mirror-writing on the front air dam was so aggressive that BMW had to remove it after public complaints.
Only 502 Evo IIs were ever built, and its outrageous rear wing was derived directly from DTM racing — making it one of the most collectible and aggressive-looking Mercedes sedans of all time.
The 959 was the most technologically advanced car of the 1980s — it pioneered electronic all-wheel drive, sequential turbocharging, and tire pressure monitoring years before anyone else.
The Carrera GT's V10 engine was originally designed for a cancelled Le Mans race car — Porsche repurposed it for the road, creating one of the most raw and visceral supercars ever made.
The Delta Integrale won six consecutive WRC Manufacturers' Championships from 1987 to 1992 — a record of dominance that has never been matched in the history of world rallying.
The F40 was the last Ferrari personally approved by Enzo Ferrari before his death — built with no ABS, no power steering, and Kevlar body panels so thin you could see the weave.
The Miura is widely considered the world's first supercar — its transverse mid-mounted V12 layout was so revolutionary that it defined the supercar template that every manufacturer follows today.
Only 36 Ferrari 250 GTOs were ever built — making it the most valuable car in the world, with examples selling at auction for over $48 million.
Only 18 Alfa Romeo 33 Stradales were ever made — its race-derived V8 revved to 10,000 RPM in 1967, and many consider it the most beautiful car ever designed.
The Pantera combined Italian styling with a Ford 351 Cleveland V8 — Elvis Presley famously owned one and allegedly shot it with a pistol when it wouldn't start.
The MC12 shared its chassis with the Ferrari Enzo but was actually longer — only 50 were built for the road, and its GT racing version won three consecutive FIA GT Championships.
Horacio Pagani hand-built the first Zonda prototype in a tiny workshop — using a Mercedes V12 engine and carbon fibre techniques he learned while working at Lamborghini on the Countach.
The 1963 split-window Corvette Stingray is one of the most iconic American cars ever built — the split rear window was only offered for one year, making it one of the most sought-after Corvettes.
Carroll Shelby stuffed Ford's massive 427 V8 into a lightweight AC Ace body — the result was so brutally fast that it terrified professional racing drivers and became an instant legend.
The GTO is widely credited with starting the American muscle car era — Pontiac engineers secretly created it by dropping a large V8 into a mid-size Tempest, bypassing GM's own corporate ban.
The Z/28 was created specifically to beat the Ford Mustang in Trans-Am racing — its high-revving 302 V8 was exactly at the 305 cubic inch displacement limit, built to dominate on the track.
Henry Ford II commissioned the GT40 out of spite after Ferrari refused his buyout offer — the GT40 then humiliated Ferrari by finishing 1-2-3 at the 1966 24 Hours of Le Mans.
The Hemi 'Cuda is the holy grail of muscle cars — fewer than 700 convertibles were built, and surviving examples have sold for over $3.5 million at auction.
The C4 ZR-1's LT5 engine was designed by Lotus and hand-built by Mercury Marine — it made the Corvette so fast that Chevrolet had to put a valet key that limited it to 210hp.
The DMC-12's stainless steel body panels were unpainted and couldn't be conventionally repaired — but it was Back to the Future that made this underwhelming sports car an eternal pop culture icon.
The 2005 Ford GT was a modern tribute to the legendary GT40 — its supercharged V8 and retro-futuristic design made it an instant collector's item that has only appreciated in value.
The DB5 became the most famous car in cinema history as James Bond's car in Goldfinger — its machine guns, ejector seat, and revolving number plates made it the ultimate movie car.
Enzo Ferrari himself called the E-Type 'the most beautiful car ever made' — high praise from the man who built Ferraris, and a sentiment that most car enthusiasts still agree with today.
The McLaren F1 held the world's fastest production car record for over a decade — Gordon Murray used a gold-lined engine bay for heat reflection and a centre driving position inspired by racing.
The Sagaris had no ABS, no traction control, and no airbags — TVR believed that the best safety device was a skilled driver, making it one of the most terrifying yet thrilling cars ever built.
The Lotus Esprit became a Bond car in 'The Spy Who Loved Me' — its Giugiaro-designed wedge shape was so futuristic that the submarine version in the film seemed almost believable.
The Defender's basic design remained virtually unchanged for 67 years — from 1948 to 2016, it served militaries, farmers, and explorers in every corner of the world.
The 205 GTI is considered the greatest hot hatch ever made by many enthusiasts — its razor-sharp handling and lightweight chassis set a benchmark that few front-wheel-drive cars have ever matched.
The Alpine A110 won the inaugural World Rally Championship in 1973 — its fibreglass body was so light that drivers could literally push the car out of snowbanks by hand.
Renault took a humble shopping car and mounted the engine behind the driver, creating a mid-engined homologation special — the 5 Turbo looked like a normal Renault 5 that had been to the gym.
The EB110 featured a quad-turbocharged V12 and carbon fibre monocoque years before anyone else — but the company went bankrupt in 1995, making surviving examples incredibly rare and valuable.
Christian von Koenigsegg started building his dream supercar in a Swedish barn at age 22 — the CC8S was the first production car from his company and immediately set speed records.
The boxy Volvo 240 Turbo shocked the European Touring Car Championship by beating BMWs and Rovers — proving that a car shaped like a brick could be a genuine racing weapon.
The Saab 900 Turbo was one of the first turbocharged production cars — designed by aircraft engineers, it featured a cockpit-like wraparound dashboard and an ignition between the seats.
The Monaro GTS 350 was Australia's answer to the American muscle car — it dominated Bathurst racing in the late 1960s and remains one of the most iconic Australian cars ever built.
